A multicenter, randomized, patient-assessor-blinded, sham-controlled clinical trial conducted in 2013 by de Castro Moura C, de Cássia Lopes Chaves E, Couto Machado Chianca T, Ruginsk SG, Alves Nogueira D, and Iunes DH evaluated the effects of auricular acupuncture on chronic pain in adults with back musculoskeletal disorders. 2. In 2019, Kim H, Mawla I, Lee J, and colleagues demonstrated that reduced tactile acuity in patients with chronic low back pain is associated with structural neuroplasticity in the primary somatosensory cortex. This neuroplasticity was shown to be modulated by acupuncture therapy. 3. Kong JT, Puetz C, Tian L, and others conducted a randomized clinical trial in 2020 comparing the effects of electroacupuncture versus sham treatment on changes in pain severity among adults with chronic low back pain. 4. Ushinohama A and colleagues, in a 2016 randomized controlled trial, investigated the impact of a single session of ear acupuncture on pain intensity and postural control in individuals with chronic low back pain. 5. Molsberger AF, Mau J, Pawelec DB, and Winkler J conducted a randomized, blinded, controlled trial in 2002 with a three-month follow-up to determine whether acupuncture improves the orthopedic management of chronic low back pain. 6. Martín-Corrales C, Bautista IV, Méndez-Mera JE, and colleagues, in a 2020 randomized clinical trial, assessed the benefits of adding gluteal dry needling to a four-week physical exercise program in a population with chronic low back pain. 7. Koppenhaver SL, Weaver AM, Randall TL, and others conducted a double-blind, randomized controlled trial in 2021 using shear wave elastography to evaluate the effect of dry needling on lumbar muscle stiffness in patients with low back pain. 8. Kerr DP, Walsh DM, and Baxter D, in a 2003 blinded randomized controlled trial, examined the role of acupuncture in the management of chronic low back pain. 9. The German Acupuncture Trials (GERAC) for chronic low back pain, conducted in 2007, was a randomized, multicenter, blinded, parallel-group trial involving three groups. 10. Huang Z, Liu S, Zhou J, Yao Q, and Liu Z, in a 2019 randomized controlled sham acupuncture trial, evaluated the efficacy and safety of acupuncture for chronic discogenic sciatica. 11. Brinkhaus B, Witt CM, Jena S, and colleagues conducted a randomized controlled trial in 2006 to assess the effects of acupuncture in patients with chronic low back pain. 12. Cherkin DC, Sherman KJ, Avins AL, and others, in a 2009 randomized trial, compared acupuncture, simulated acupuncture, and usual care for chronic low back pain. 13. Cho YJ, Song YK, Cha YY, and colleagues conducted a multicenter, randomized, patient-assessor-blinded, sham-controlled clinical trial in 2013 to evaluate acupuncture for chronic low back pain. 14. The WHO guideline on the non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults includes a summary of evidence regarding the benefits and harms of acupuncture compared to no intervention or interventions isolating the effect of acupuncture. This guideline considers community-dwelling adults, including older adults aged 60 years and above, with or without leg pain. 15. The Brief Pain Inventory (BPI), confidence interval (CI), EuroQol 5 Dimensions (EQ-5D), Japanese Orthopedic Association (JOA) score, mean difference (MD), Mental Component Summary (MCS), Optimal Information Size (OIS), odds ratio (OR), numerical rating scale (NRS), Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), Physical Component Summary (PCS), Roland Morris Disability Questionnaire (RMDQ), Short Form Health Survey (SF-36), standardized mean difference (SMD), Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), and Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) were used as outcome measures in these trials. 16. Risk of bias was categorized as not serious, serious, or very serious based on the proportion of weight derived from trials with low or high risk of bias. Inconsistency was evaluated based on the similarity of point estimates, overlap of confidence intervals, and statistical heterogeneity (I² values). Indirectness was assessed based on the relevance of evidence to the PICO question and the settings of the trials. Imprecision was determined by sample size adequacy and whether confidence intervals crossed the null or clinically important thresholds. 17. Some trials were excluded from meta-analyses due to reporting within-group change scores rather than between-group comparisons. For example, de Castro Moura 2019 (111 participants) and Weiß 2013 (160 participants) were rated as having a high risk of bias and showed no significant differences between groups. 18. Downgrading of evidence occurred in cases of serious or very serious concerns regarding risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, or imprecision. For instance, trials with small sample sizes or high heterogeneity (e.g., I² = 97%) were downgraded due to imprecision or inconsistency. 19. Publication bias was considered not serious when undetected but serious or very serious when strongly suspected. 20. The overall findings from these trials consistently demonstrated a reduction in pain with acupuncture, though the quality of evidence varied depending on trial design, sample size, and methodological rigor.
